claims.text: Nanoscale lattice distortions caused by atomic size mismatch are the primary control of strength and deformation behavior in multi-component concentrated alloys.
Nanoscale lattice distortions increase local energy barriers for dislocation motion.
Increasing atomic size variance creates greater localized lattice distortion.
The localized lattice distortions act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
The elevated barrier to dislocation movement increases yield strength.
Atomic-size-mismatch-induced lattice distortion modifies plastic deformation and work-hardening behavior.
The proposed effect is more pronounced when dislocation slip is the primary mode of plasticity.
Alloys engineered to have greater atomic size mismatch will have higher yield strength than a reduced-mismatch baseline.
Alloys engineered to have greater atomic size mismatch will exhibit altered work-hardening behavior relative to the baseline.
A significant relative increase in yield strength would indicate that lattice distortion dominates alternative strengthening mechanisms.
The comparison can isolate atomic size mismatch by holding grain size, processing history, and phase distribution constant.
The hypothesis is expected to apply to single-phase or nearly single-phase alloys when grain boundaries, phase transformations, and diffusion do not dominate deformation.
The hypothesis may not apply at high temperatures or in alloys containing significant second-phase precipitates.
Short-range order, secondary phases, and other kinetic phenomena may also modulate strength and deformation.
Failure to observe a statistically significant yield-strength increase or a measurable work-hardening change in the high-mismatch samples would falsify the dominant-lattice-distortion hypothesis.
Evidence that short-range order or particulate strengthening dominates the stress–strain response would falsify the dominant-lattice-distortion hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention requires changing composition or substituting atoms to alter atomic size mismatch, whereas the baseline says the overall elemental composition is identical. Element substitution cannot generally preserve an identical elemental composition; the intended constraint may instead be similar concentration, phase constitution, or processing.
